# APPROACH TO ACUTE MENINGITIS

Meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges and tissues surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It is characterized by an abnormal amount of white blood cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and symptoms include headache, fever, mental status changes, nuchal rigidity, and nausea.

# Acute Meningitis

The sudden onset of meningeal symptoms within hours to days caused by several infectious etiologies, including bacterial, viral, fungal and protozoa, as well as non-infectious etiologies. Bacterial meningitis is the most common type of meningitis, accounting for up to 90% of cases where a CSF culture was obtained prior to starting antimicrobials. Non-bacterial meningitis is commonly referred to as aseptic meningitis (refer to "Negative CSF culture" below for recommendations).

Patients with acute bacterial meningitis often have severe symptoms and present soon after onset of infection. The relationship between predisposing factors and common bacterial pathogen are listed below.

# Predisposing Factors and Common Bacterial Pathogens

\*Age 2-50 years - [S. pneumoniae](meningitis-with-streptococcus-pneumoniae), [N. meningitidis](meningitis-with-neisseria-meningitidis)

\*Age > 50 years - S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, [L. monocytogenes](listeria-monocytogenes-meningitis), aerobic gram-negative bacilli

\*Immunocompromised state - S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, L. monocytogenes, aerobic gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa)

\*Basilar skull fracture - S. pneumoniae: H. influenzae, group A and beta-hemolytic streptococci

\*Head trauma: after neurosurgery - Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci (especially Staphylococcus epidermidis), aerobic gram-negative bacilli (including P. aeruginosa)

# Initial Management of Suspected Acute Bacterial Meningitis

Once a diagnosis of acute bacterial meningitis is considered likely, antimicrobials should be initiated as soon as possible. Two blood cultures should be drawn. Lumbar puncture (LP) should be performed in nearly all patients to obtain CSF for establishing diagnosis and determining infectious organism/susceptibility. Computed tomography (CT) should be performed prior to LP in some patients (see list below). If CT must be obtained prior to LP or there is another delay in performing LP, empiric antimicrobials should not be delayed and initiated immediately after obtaining blood cultures only.

Relative LP contraindications (no absolute contraindications exist):
Anticoagulation therapy or bleeding disorder, spinal epidural abscess, raised intracranial pressure.

Computed tomography scan should be performed prior to lumbar puncture in cases
with the following:
Immunocompromise, history of CNS disease, new onset seizure, papilledema, abnormal level of consciousness, focal neurologic deficit.

# LP and CSF Analysis

LP opening pressure is often elevated in bacterial meningitis. CSF findings characteristic of bacterial meningitis include CSF glucose <40mg/dL, CSF to serum glucose ratio </=0.4, CSF protein concentration >/=200 mg/dL and CSF WBC >1000 microL.

# Treatment Based on CSF Isolated Organism

When infectious organism is identified, adjust antimicrobials to optimize therapy:
[S. pneumoniae](meningitis-with-streptococcus-pneumoniae)

[N. meningitidis](meningitis-with-neisseria-meningitidis)

[L. monocytogenes](listeria-monocytogenes-meningitis)

[E. Coli, Pseudomonas, or another organism](meningitis-with-e-coli-pseudomonas-or-other-organism)

# Negative CSF Culture

Patients who have a negative CSF culture but have symptoms and CSF findings consistent with bacterial meningitis should be treated based on likely pathogen.

Patients with negative CSF culture, symptoms of acute meningitis but have labs inconsistent with bacterial meningitis should be considered to have aseptic meningitis. Aseptic meningitis is caused by a variety of non-bacterial infectious etiologies and non-infectious etiologies. Consult Infectious Disease for more information.
